name: Protein-heavy growth diet

lead: Adolescents in height communities eat plenty of protein and calories, often from meat, dairy and eggs, so that nutrition does not limit growth and they reach their full genetic height. Unlike many height ideas, it relates to a documented determinant of growth: childhood nutrition.

Growth depends on adequate energy and amino acids alongside genetics and hormones. Chronic childhood malnutrition is documented to delay growth and reduce adult height, national average height correlates with protein quality, and Guatemalan Maya children raised in the US were about 10 cm taller than peers in Guatemala, attributed largely to better nutrition and health care. Studies of extra protein in already well-nourished teens were not found.

paras: People build meals around protein foods such as meat, dairy, eggs and fish, eat enough total calories, and pair it with sleep and training during the growth years. Results are measured over the full course of puberty rather than weeks.
A balanced diet is ordinary; people with kidney or metabolic conditions follow medical guidance on protein. Extreme diets carry their own nutritional risks.

chain: Adequate protein and calories in puberty
angle.text: Eating enough protein and calories through puberty supplies what growth needs, helping you reach your full genetic height. Childhood nutrition is a documented determinant of growth; whether protein beyond normal needs adds more has not been tested.

lead: A protein-heavy growth diet is an approach discussed in height communities in which adolescents eat adequate or high amounts of protein and calories, often from meat, dairy and eggs, to reach their maximum genetic height. Unlike many height claims, it relates to a documented determinant of growth: childhood nutrition.[1]

Reference sources describe adult height as 60 to 80 percent heritable, and state that chronic malnutrition in childhood and adolescence can delay growth and reduce adult height.[1] National average height is described as correlating with protein quality, with countries eating more meat, dairy, eggs and fish tending to be taller.[1] A study of Guatemalan Maya children found those raised in the United States about 10 cm taller than peers in Guatemala, attributed largely to better nutrition and health care.[1]
Sources do not report that eating more protein than needed in an already well-nourished adolescent increases height beyond genetic potential.

paras: Proponents recommend sufficient calories and protein-rich foods during puberty so that nutrition is not a limiting factor on growth. Some also discuss related nutrients such as calcium and vitamin D.

Childhood and adolescence are described as critical periods in which undernutrition can reduce adult height even without a medical condition.[1] Population comparisons link taller average stature with diets richer in animal protein, though large differences between populations may reflect genetics, lifestyle or both.[1] Growth is described as ending on average around age 15 or 16 in females and 18 to 19 in males.[1]

No studies found testing a protein-heavy diet specifically as a height-maximising protocol in well-nourished adolescents. Population and malnutrition research, summarised in reference works, links poor childhood nutrition with reduced adult height.[1]

lore.intro: In height forums, adequate nutrition is often described as the most defensible lever for teenagers, in contrast with supplements or devices.
